query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a copper‐wetted (or compatible high‐entropy alloy) interlayer via vapor deposition prior to consolidation will create near‐perfect interfacial bonding with the copper matrix, thereby minimizing voids and phase separation and enhancing thermal transport under irradiation while preserving mechanical durability compared to conventional SPS or mechanical alloying routes.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles (or connected W regions) embedded in a copper matrix produced by typical powder metallurgy approaches that suffer from interfacial voids, phase separation, and defects affecting thermal transport.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform vapor deposition coating on tungsten particles (using a copper-wetting interlayer or a suitable high-entropy alloy layer) before consolidating the W–Cu composite by spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: The process should use controlled vapor deposition to ensure uniform, conformal coatings on tungsten particles, followed by SPS under conditions (rapid heating/cooling) that preserve the nano-/fine-grained microstructure. Testing should be conducted under irradiation and high-thermal flux conditions representative of fusion-reactor joint environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal coating layer on W particles that promotes enhanced diffusion and metallurgical bonding with the Cu matrix, effectively eliminating voids and discontinuities at the interface.
generation.mechanism: The coating improves wettability and interdiffusion during sintering, leading to defect-free, continuous interfaces between tungsten and copper. This reduces phase separation and void formation, thereby establishing more efficient thermal pathways under irradiation while maintaining mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventional W–Cu composite (e.g., one produced by direct SPS or mechanical alloying without coating), the vapor-coated version will exhibit significantly reduced void fractions and improved interfacial bonding, resulting in enhanced thermal conductivity and maintained mechanical durability under simulated irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional powder metallurgical processing of W–Cu composites via SPS or mechanical alloying without any pre-coating, which is known to produce voids and phase separations that impair thermal transport.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective for powder sizes and sintering conditions typical for fabricating fusion-reactor joints. It is applicable within the temperature and irradiation regimes common to fusion plasma-facing components.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating material, thickness, and processing parameters require further optimization. In addition, the long-term stability of the interlayer under continuous irradiation is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set using tungsten particles pre-coated via vapor deposition with a copper-wetting (or HEA) interlayer, and a control set using uncoated tungsten particles. Consolidate both sets by spark plasma sintering under identical conditions. Subject the consolidated samples to thermal cycling and ion irradiation (using Ar+, He+, or D+ beams) that simulate fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Examination of interfacial bonding and void fractions via SEM/TEM
Thermal conductivity measurements before and after irradiation
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., compression and flexural strength) pre- and post-irradiation
Assessment of microstructural homogeneity using XRD or EBSD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vapor-coated W–Cu composite does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in void reduction, interfacial bonding, thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability under irradiation compared to the control sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Powder milling not only increases contamination due to wear of milling media,  but it makes powders susceptible to oxidation as well. This paper presents the potential of elemental powder mixing followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) given the ability of this process to consolidate the powder into a fine-grained material with a controlled structure and high density while saving time due to the short soaking period and high heating and cooling rates, , , , , , for the fabrication of a HEA and its derivative alloys for high-temperature and plasma-facing applications.

Casting [] and powder metallurgy [] are two common methods for preparing HEAs. For casting, there are two kinds of defects which are the vaporization of low melting-point elements and the elements segregation in the ingot []. For powder metallurgy, the HEAs can be prepared by MA and then consolidated. The HEAs powders prepared by MA are uniform and fine, and even form nanocrystalline. Hence a rapid sintering is needed to maintain this microstructure []. SPS is a new field-assisted sintering technique which can effectively suppress the grain coarsening by rapid heating and efficient densification in a few minutes [,,]. Compared with MA, gas atomization can produce more homogeneous powders. The preparation of HEAs powders by gas atomization is a rapid solidification process [], in which grain growth and element segregation are inhibited, and the high cooling rate even leads to the formation of an amorphous phase []. In the previous studies, two classical HEAs, CoCrFeNiMn with a single FCC phase and AlCoCrFeNi with a single BCC phase, have been extensively studied.
